stem: Three packages in your monorepo each keep the same 210-line accessibility standard pasted into their own CLAUDE.md. The design systems team has revised the standard twice since, the three copies now disagree about focus-trap rules, and Claude generates different modal markup depending on which package an engineer is working in. The canonical document is committed at docs/standards/accessibility.md. What is the most maintainable fix?

options.text: Move the full 210 lines into the root CLAUDE.md and delete the three package copies, so every session reads the same text.
Keep the three copies and add a CI check that fails the build whenever a package copy differs from docs/standards/accessibility.md.
Replace the pasted copies with @import docs/standards/accessibility.md in each package CLAUDE.md that needs it.
Move the standard into a skill under .claude/skills/ and ask engineers to invoke it before any UI work.

explanation: @import lets each package's CLAUDE.md pull in the committed canonical file, so there is one source of truth and each package loads only the standards its maintainers actually need.

why.A: Loads 210 lines of UI rules into every session in the repository, including packages that render no UI, and leaves a fourth copy diverging from docs/standards/accessibility.md.
why.B: Automates policing the duplication instead of removing it; three copies still have to be edited on every revision.
why.D: A skill loads only when invoked, so a standard that must apply to all UI work would depend on someone remembering it.

stem: The team standard is 4-space indentation. It is on the internal wiki and enforced by the linter, but appears nowhere in the repository's Claude Code configuration. One engineer's sessions keep producing 2-space code that the linter then rewrites. Running /memory in that session lists the project CLAUDE.md plus their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which carries a line from a previous job saying to indent with 2 spaces. Which two changes fix this? (Select 2)

options.text: Add the 4-space rule to the project CLAUDE.md, so every clone of the repository carries it.
Restate the rule in capitals at the top of the project CLAUDE.md so it outweighs the engineer's personal instruction.
Have the whole team delete ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, since a personal memory file is what caused this.
Have that engineer remove the 2-space line from their ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which applies to all their sessions.

explanation: The standard has to exist at project level to reach every clone, and the contradicting user-level line has to go, because it keeps applying to that engineer's sessions in every repository they open.

why.B: Leaves the contradiction in place and relies on emphasis to win it, which is not a guarantee.
why.C: Over-broad: personal files legitimately hold per-user preferences, and only one line is the problem.

stem: A frozen legacy service occupies services/legacy-billing/ and nothing else: about 400 files of JavaScript, SQL and shell scripts. Its conventions contradict the rest of the monorepo, callback-style error handling, a bespoke logging wrapper and no async/await, and they are meant to apply to every file in that tree whatever its extension and to nothing outside it. Engineers move between this tree and the modern packages within a single session. Where do these conventions belong?

options.text: In the root CLAUDE.md, under a heading stating that the rules apply only to files in services/legacy-billing/.
In services/legacy-billing/CLAUDE.md, the directory-level file for that tree.
In .claude/rules/legacy-billing.md scoped with paths: ["**/*.js"], the extension most of the tree uses.
In a skill under .claude/skills/ that engineers invoke before touching anything in the legacy tree.

explanation: A directory-level CLAUDE.md applies to work in that directory tree and nothing else, which fits conventions whose boundary is a directory rather than a file type.

why.A: Loads the legacy rules into every session in the monorepo and leaves the model to judge when the heading applies instead of matching the path.
why.C: Scopes by extension, so it misses the SQL and shell files inside the tree and matches JavaScript everywhere outside it.
why.D: On-demand invocation for conventions that must govern every edit in the tree, so coverage depends on someone remembering to invoke it.

stem: A new pipeline step has Claude Code draft release notes from the merge commits of a release branch. The same command finishes in under a minute on an engineer's laptop. In CI the step prints its banner, produces nothing further, and is killed by the job's 30-minute timeout, with no error in the runner log. The prompt and the commit list are already passed to the command as arguments, the runner has no TTY, and nothing is attached to the job's stdin. What is the fix?

options.text: Raise the job timeout to 60 minutes so the generation step has room to finish its work.
Add --output-format json so the step emits a parseable result rather than an interactive display.
Pipe the list of merge commits into the command on stdin so the process has input to read.
Add the -p flag so Claude Code runs non-interactively and exits once the prompt is answered.

explanation: The -p (print) flag is what runs Claude Code non-interactively in a pipeline; without it the session waits for interactive input that a runner with no TTY never provides, so the job hangs until the timeout kills it.

why.A: The step is not slow, it is waiting for input, so a longer timeout only makes the hang last longer.
why.B: --output-format json shapes the result of a non-interactive run; on its own it does not stop the session waiting for input.
why.C: The prompt is already an argument, so there is nothing for stdin to supply, and reading input does not make the session non-interactive.

stem: Your pipeline step runs claude -p "/security-scan $CHANGED_FILES" and fails with an unknown command error on every run, while the same invocation works for the two engineers who wrote it. Both of them have security-scan.md in ~/.claude/commands/. The team wants a single definition that engineers and the pipeline both use and that is reviewed like any other change in the repository. What is the fix?

options.text: Move security-scan.md into .claude/commands/ in the repository so the CI checkout has it.
Add a pipeline setup step that writes the command file into the runner's ~/.claude/commands/ directory before the scan.
Drop the slash command and inline the full checklist prompt into the pipeline definition instead.
Add --resume to the invocation so the job continues in a session where the command is already defined.

explanation: Project-scoped commands live in .claude/commands/ and travel with the repository, so a CI checkout and every engineer get the same definition.

why.B: Recreates a personal-scope file on a throwaway runner, leaving the definition outside the repository where nobody reviews it.
why.C: Abandons the shared definition, so the pipeline copy and the two local copies drift apart.
why.D: --resume continues a previous session; it does not make a command definition available to a new one.

stem: Your team's /scaffold-module skill needs a module name and a target package before it can generate anything. Two problems in the last month: engineers invoke it bare roughly half the time and it guesses a target package, and on one run it cleared an existing directory through Bash before regenerating it, destroying uncommitted work. The skill only needs to read templates and write new files. Which two frontmatter changes address these? (Select 2)

options.text: context: fork, so a wrong guess and anything the skill deletes stay inside an isolated sub-agent context.
argument-hint naming the module name and target package, so a bare invocation prompts for them.
allowed-tools listing only the read and write tools it needs, with Bash left out.
A rewritten description stating that the skill always needs two arguments and must never delete anything.

explanation: argument-hint prompts for the parameters a bare invocation is missing, and allowed-tools removes the capability that destroyed the work rather than asking the skill not to use it.

why.A: context: fork isolates conversation context, not filesystem effects, and it does nothing about missing arguments.
why.D: Prose in the skill cannot guarantee either outcome when both have a declarative frontmatter field for it.

stem: Your /options skill exists to brainstorm: given a problem it returns four or five candidate designs with trade-offs, typically 6,000 words. Engineers run it, choose one, then implement in the same session. Reviewers now see rejected ideas bleeding into the code, retry logic from a discarded option in one pull request and naming from another. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Add context: fork to the skill so it runs in an isolated sub-agent context and returns only its result.
Set allowed-tools to read-only tools so the brainstorming skill cannot write any code itself.
Ask engineers to run /compact after choosing an option and before starting the implementation.
Split the skill so it produces one option per invocation and engineers run only the ones they want.

explanation: context: fork is designed for exploratory skills like brainstorming alternatives, keeping the discarded options out of the main conversation that then writes the code.

why.B: The skill is not writing the code; the main session is, and the contamination is context rather than tool access.
why.C: Compaction summarizes rather than removes, so rejected designs can survive into the summary, and it depends on engineers remembering.
why.D: The comparison is the point of the skill, and each invocation still lands its text in the main session.

stem: Storybook files sit next to the components they document: 340 files matching *.stories.tsx across 12 component directories plus a separate examples app. The design systems team put a CLAUDE.md with the story-writing conventions in each of the 12 directories. Three of those copies have drifted, the examples app was never covered, and a directory added last week has no conventions at all. What is the most maintainable way to apply the conventions?

options.text: Move the conventions into the root CLAUDE.md under a Storybook heading and let Claude apply them when it recognises a story file.
Keep the per-directory files and add a lint rule that fails when any of them differs from the canonical copy.
Put the conventions in a skill under .claude/skills/ and have engineers invoke it before writing stories.
One .claude/rules/stories.md with frontmatter paths: ["**/*.stories.tsx"].

explanation: A glob-scoped rule follows the file type wherever it lives, so new directories and the examples app are covered automatically from a single file.

why.A: Relies on the model inferring which section applies rather than matching the path, and loads UI rules in every session.
why.B: Keeps 12 copies in maintenance and still covers no directory that is created later.
why.C: A skill has to be invoked, so coverage depends on someone remembering it for every story file.

stem: Your .claude/rules/ directory holds six topic files. Five carry a paths field in their YAML frontmatter. graphql-schema.md, 380 lines of resolver and schema naming rules, has no frontmatter at all, and engineers see it loaded in every session: someone editing a deployment shell script had the resolver naming rules applied to a helper function. The conventions genuinely only concern files under schema/ and any file with a .graphql extension. What is the fix?

options.text: Move the content into a skill so it is loaded on demand only when someone is doing schema work.
Add frontmatter to graphql-schema.md with paths: ["schema/**/*", "**/*.graphql"].
Move the file to schema/CLAUDE.md so that it applies to that directory tree and nothing else.
Cut the file down to about 80 lines so the cost of loading it in every session is acceptable.

explanation: A rules file without a paths field is not path-scoped, so adding the globs makes it load only while matching files are being worked on.

why.A: Trades automatic activation by file path for manual invocation, so schema work without the invocation gets no conventions.
why.C: A directory-bound answer to a file-type problem: .graphql files outside schema/ would be left uncovered.
why.D: Reduces the volume but the rules still load during work they have nothing to do with.

stem: A rules file api-conventions.md, 600 lines on HTTP handlers covering error envelopes, pagination and status codes, carries paths: ["**/*.ts"]. Since it landed, review has caught error-envelope wrapping added to a build script, pagination boilerplate in a database seed helper, and handler conventions applied inside test doubles. Every real handler is either under src/api/ or named *.handler.ts. What is the smallest change that fixes this?

options.text: Add a paragraph at the top of api-conventions.md stating that the rules apply only to HTTP handlers.
Split the 600 lines into one rules file per convention, each still scoped with paths: ["**/*.ts"].
Narrow the glob to paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts", "**/*.handler.ts"].
Replace the rules file with a CLAUDE.md placed in src/api/ so the conventions apply there only.

explanation: The rule is loading for files it was never meant to govern, so the fix is to make the glob describe the handlers instead of every TypeScript file.

why.A: Puts a prose caveat inside a rule that still loads for every TypeScript file, relying on inference where matching is available.
why.B: Reorganizes the content without changing when any of it loads.
why.D: Misses every handler named *.handler.ts that lives outside src/api/.

stem: One file, src/sync/reconcile.ts, decides what happens when the same record is edited on two devices while both are offline. Three approaches are on the table: last write wins on a timestamp, a per-field merge, and keeping both versions for the user to resolve. They differ in what each client has to store, whether a merge can be undone, and what the mobile team must build to match. Nobody has chosen yet. How should this be approached?

options.text: Direct execution, since the change is confined to one file with no other call sites to update.
Plan mode, to settle which of the three approaches the clients will be built around.
Direct execution of all three, then compare the finished diffs and keep whichever reads best.
Direct execution of the timestamp approach, as the smallest change, revising it later if needed.

explanation: Plan mode is for work with several valid approaches and architectural consequences; the number of files touched is not the criterion, and this choice commits every client to a data model.

why.A: Treats scope as the deciding factor, but a one-file change can still carry a decision other teams have to build against.
why.C: Spends three implementations on a decision that comparing the approaches would settle, and the real differences are in stored state rather than in the diffs.
why.D: Chooses by size rather than fit, and a reconciliation model is expensive to reverse once clients hold data in its shape.

stem: Retro data for last sprint: 19 tasks, of which 14 were single-function changes with a cause already named in a stack trace or a ticket, such as a missing null check or a wrong status code. Team policy sends everything through plan mode. Median time from opening a session to the first edit was 22 minutes, and engineers describe reading two-page plans for four-line fixes. Three of the 19 were multi-file work with competing approaches. How should the team adjust the policy?

options.text: Use direct execution for changes that are already scoped and understood, keeping plan mode for the multi-file work.
Keep plan mode everywhere as a safety policy, but ask for much shorter plans on the small tasks.
Drop plan mode entirely and rely on code review to catch structural mistakes on the larger tasks.
Keep plan mode everywhere and cut the cost by pasting the approved plan into a fresh session to implement it.

explanation: Plan mode earns its cost on architectural or multi-approach work; a single-function fix with a named cause is the textbook case for direct execution.

why.B: Shortening the output leaves the exploration overhead in place on tasks that need no exploration.
why.C: Removes the mode precisely where it pays off, pushing architectural risk into review where rework is expensive.
why.D: Adds process to every task without addressing that most of these tasks never needed a plan.

stem: Phase one of a four-phase documentation task inventories every scheduled job in a 900-file service, and you are running it through the Explore subagent to keep the Grep and Read output out of the main session. Phase three has to document each job's schedule, its owning module and the queue it writes to. On the first attempt Explore returned a three-paragraph prose overview, so phase three re-read 40 files to recover those specifics and the raw output landed in the main session anyway. What should change?

options.text: Run phase one in the main session after all, since its findings are needed in detail later.
Have phase three invoke the Explore subagent again for each job it needs to document.
Ask for a longer overview so that more of the detail survives into the main session.
Ask Explore to return a structured record per job with schedule, owning module and queue.

explanation: Explore preserves the main conversation by returning a summary, so the summary has to carry the fields the later phases need; an unstructured overview forces the raw reads back into the session.

why.A: Puts the 900-file search output into the main conversation, which is the cost the subagent exists to avoid.
why.B: Repeats the discovery once per job, paying for the same exploration many times over.
why.C: Length is not the issue: an overview can grow long and still omit the queue and the owning module.

stem: Review of a generated service module turned up six unrelated defects across four files: a typo in a log message, a missing await on a fire-and-forget call, an off-by-one in a paginator, a wrong HTTP status, an unused import and a stale comment. No two of the fixes touch the same code path. You sent all six in one message and got back a patch that fixed four, silently skipped two, and refactored an unrelated helper along the way. What is the better way to work through them?

options.text: Send the same six-item list again with more detail per item and an instruction to change nothing else.
Ask for a rewrite of the module with all six behaviours corrected in the new version.
Fix them one at a time, verifying each before moving on, since the fixes do not interact.
Split them into two messages by severity so the important fixes land before the cosmetic ones.

explanation: A single message is for issues whose fixes interact; independent issues iterate more reliably one at a time, because each fix can be verified before the next is requested.

why.A: Detail was not the problem: the same batched shape is what produced the two silent skips.
why.B: Expands a six-line set of independent fixes into a full rewrite and a diff nobody can review.
why.D: Still batches independent changes into one pass; ordering by severity does not address the skipping.

stem: Documentation stubs have to be generated from route handlers in the team's house style: a one-line summary in imperative mood, a parameter table ordered as the handler declares them, and every error code the handler can return listed under its own heading. You have described that style in prose twice, more carefully the second time. The first attempt wrote summaries in the third person; the second reordered the parameter table alphabetically and folded the error codes into the summary paragraph. Thirty endpoints on the previous service were documented by hand and are still in the repository. What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Describe the style a third time as a numbered list of rules for tense, parameter order and error codes.
Supply two or three of the hand-documented handlers with the stub written for each.
Have Claude interview you about the house style before it generates any further stubs.
Ask for three candidate formats for a single handler and pick whichever is closest to the style.

explanation: Concrete input and output pairs are the most effective way to communicate a transformation that prose has already failed to pin down twice, and the hand-documented endpoints are exactly that material.

why.A: A third pass of prose in a tidier shape, when what failed twice was interpretation of prose rather than a missing rule.
why.C: The interview pattern surfaces requirements you cannot state; here the style is known and already demonstrated in thirty documented endpoints.
why.D: Settles the format for one handler without fixing the rule the remaining endpoints are generated against.

stem: Your currency formatter fails 3 of 60 tests. For four rounds you have replied "still failing, please fix" and received three speculative rewrites, each of which changed rounding logic that was already correct. The test runner's output names the three failing tests and prints, for one of them, that 1.005 was expected to format as "1.01" but came out as "1.00". What should you send next?

options.text: The failing test names with the expected and actual values straight from the runner output.
A more careful prose description of the rounding behaviour the formatter is supposed to have.
A request to rewrite the formatter from scratch so it satisfies the whole suite this time.
Ten further test cases around the rounding boundary so the pattern becomes clearer.

explanation: Test-driven iteration works by sharing the actual failures; the runner output already isolates the defect, and four rounds of describing it have produced only guesses.

why.B: Prose is what has failed four times running, and the exact values are already available.
why.C: Discards behaviour that passes 57 tests in order to fix three cases.
why.D: Adds work to narrow down something the existing output has already narrowed down.

stem: Your review job runs claude -p with --output-format json and the pipeline reads the JSON envelope without trouble. The posting script still cannot place inline comments: the findings arrive inside one result string as prose, sometimes numbered, sometimes as markdown bullets, occasionally as a paragraph naming three files at once. Roughly 20% of runs post nothing at all. What is the correct change?

options.text: Keep the current output and make the posting script's regular expressions stricter about the shapes it accepts.
Ask in the prompt for numbered findings, one per line, in the form path:line:severity:message.
Add --json-schema defining an array of findings with file, line, severity and message.
Post one summary comment per pull request instead of trying to place comments inline.

explanation: --output-format json gives a JSON envelope but not a shape for what is inside it; --json-schema constrains the findings themselves, which is what the posting script needs to map to file and line.

why.A: Parsing prose with regular expressions is the source of the fragility, not something stricter patterns repair.
why.B: A formatting request shapes likelihood; a schema is what makes the output machine-parseable every run.
why.D: Abandons the inline requirement rather than meeting it, and the findings are still unstructured.

stem: Your CI review posts 30 to 40 comments per pull request and developers have started ignoring the bot. An audit of last month's comments finds two clusters: 40% repeat a finding already posted on an earlier push of the same pull request, and 25% flag patterns the team has deliberately adopted and documented on the wiki, such as raw SQL in the reporting module and the any type in the legacy adapter layer. Which two changes address these two clusters? (Select 2)

options.text: Cap the job at the ten highest-severity comments per run so the volume stays readable.
Pass the pull request's prior findings into each re-run and ask for only new or still-unaddressed issues.
Document the intentional patterns and the review criteria in the project CLAUDE.md that the CI session loads.
Run the review three times per push and post only the findings that appear in all three runs.

explanation: Prior findings in context stop the re-run from repeating comments, and the accepted patterns belong in the project CLAUDE.md so the CI-invoked session knows what is intentional rather than flagging it.

why.A: Hides output, including real findings, without touching either cause of the noise.
why.D: Consensus filtering suppresses genuine bugs that are only caught intermittently, and it triples the cost.
